A total of 34 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in October, adding more than $96 billion in value and $14.8 billion in total funding to the board. The board also reached a new record of 1,900 private companies last month, including an all-time high of more than 1,000 such startups based in the U.S.
Last month’s new unicorn cohort also highlighted how quickly this AI cycle is awarding some companies with billion-dollar-plus valuations: Half of October’s new unicorns are less than 4 years old, and nine companies that joined the board during the month did so via seed or Series A raises.
Leading industries for unicorn formation last month were frontier labs, agentic AI, aerospace and semiconductors. The U.S. accounts for 23 of the companies, while China and Korea each added three. Estonia added two, a record for the nation in a single month. Singapore, Germany and Japan each added one new unicorn.
The most valuable of the newly minted unicorns were electrical infrastructure company Axiom Solutions International , TypeSafe AI a model developer of Jev, and agentic AI assistant company Manus AI .
Familiar names topped the list of investors backing the latest cohort. Andreessen Horowitz has led rounds across seven portfolio companies over time, Sequoia Capital and General Catalyst in four companies and Eclipse three companies from this batch.
New unicorns in October 2026
Here are October’s new unicorn companies by industry segment.
AI models, assistants and agents
TypeSafe AI : San Francisco-based AI model developer TypeSafe AI raised an $870 million Series A at a $7.5 billion valuation. Andreessen Horowitz led the round, with participation from DCVC and Sequoia Capital. The 2-year-old company develops an AI model Jev for structured decision-making, helping applications automate tasks such as classification, scoring and routing with confidence estimates.
Manus AI : Singapore-based AI assistant Manus AI raised $500 million at a $4 billion valuation. Boyu Capital and IDG Capital led the round. The 3-year-old company develops general-purpose AI agents that perform tasks including research, browser automation, content creation and software development. Meta agreed to acquire Manus in December 2025, but Chinese regulators intervened and ordered the transaction reversed.
Nous Research : Austin-based Nous Research, developer of the Hermes agent, raised a $90 million Series B at a $1.5 billion valuation. Robot Ventures led the financing, with investors including Nvidia , Microsoft’s M12 , Menlo Ventures and Union Square Ventures . The 3-year-old company develops open-source AI models, agents and infrastructure for AI development and deployment. Nous Research built the open-source Hermes Agent, which it is deploying for businesses.
Upstage : South Korea-based Upstage, developer of the open-source Solar model, raised $30 million in Series C funding, reaching $1.5 billion in value. The 6-year-old company develops the Solar language models and document-processing technology that converts unstructured business information into usable data for the future of work.
Wabi : San Francisco-based personal AI assistant Wabi raised a $55 million Series A at a $1.25 billion valuation. IVP led the financing, joined by investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Forerunner and Amazon’s Alexa Fund . The 1-year-old company develops an AI personal assistant for everyday activities such as planning trips, coordinating meals and organizing tasks.
Town : San Francisco-based Town, a developer of a workforce AI assistant, raised a $108 million Series B at a $1 billion valuation. Forerunner and Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz, First Round Capital and other investors. The 2-year-old company develops personalized AI assistants that connect with workplace tools across teams to manage email, prepare meeting briefings, organize schedules and complete recurring tasks.
Aerospace, defense and space
Air Space Intelligence : Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, which makes AI software for national security, raised a $325 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation. Spark Capital led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz, Citadel Securities , Craft Ventures , Energy Impact Partners and Meritech Capital Partners . The 8-year-old company develops AI software for managing complex physical operations across aviation, defense, energy and logistics.
Xona : Burlingame, California-based Xona, which says it’s developing a better satellite navigation system, raised a $250 million Series D at a $2.45 billion valuation. Future Ventures led the round, with participation from Industrious Ventures and Woven Capital . The 7-year-old company says it’s developing a low Earth orbit satellite network to deliver precise positioning, navigation and timing services for applications including defense, transportation and autonomous systems.
Firehawk Aerospace : Dallas-based munitions manufacturer Firehawk Aerospace raised a $150 million Series D at a $1.4 billion valuation. Anthropic is seeking to secure up to $88.5 billion in its planned IPO and a concurrent private placement, potentially making it the largest-ever fundraise tied to a public market debut.
On Tuesday, the AI giant submitted an updated S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering, unveiling new details including a proposed share price range offering size. The offering could set a fully diluted valuation of up to $1.4 trillion for the San Francisco company.
Anthropic’s expected valuation comes in below earlier projections, with many investors reportedly forecasting something closer to $2 trillion. That said, even at $1.4 trillion, Anthropic would still be going public at the second-highest valuation in history, topped only by SpaceX ’s June debut.
An IPO and a private placement
The offering should also provide Anthropic with plentiful capital to pursue its expensive expansion and infrastructure investment plans.
For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic plans to sell just over 800 million shares 1 at $70 to $78 each. At the high end, that would bring in around $62.5 billion — the largest ever IPO fundraise after SpaceX’s $75 billion offering.
Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD , Broadcom , Google , Micron Technology , Microsoft , Nvidia and TSMC .
Put together, it’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut, which Anthropic is expected to do later this month on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.
Revenue and recent updates
Anthropic also recently updated its financial disclosures, showing results through September of this year.
For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. It’s an astounding growth rate, albeit Anthropic is already known for this.
The company claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026.
As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago.

candidates.title: Hugging Face CEO vows to keep fighting for open source AI after Jensen Huang’s exit
candidates.snippet: Hugging Face's CEO pledged to keep fighting for open source AI after Huang's exit, raising questions about Nvidia's $12.9 billion acquisition.
candidates.text:
Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue briefly commented on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s departure on Thursday, calling it a “really sad day.” Nvidia had announced its plan to acquire the platform for open source AI models in September for $12.9 billion, making it the second-largest acquisition in the company’s history, just behind that of chipmaker Groq’s assets for $20 billion in December 2025.
“This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!,” Delangue wrote on X.
This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day!
But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go! — clem 🤗 (@ClementDelangue) November 12, 2026
The post is interesting as it implies that Huang’s departure is potentially worrying to open source advocates, and he’s attempting to offer reassurance.
As Nvidia’s CEO, Huang was known as a strong advocate for open source AI and open-weight models, which is why there could be concerns about how a company that’s no longer under his leadership will now approach this space.
After Nvidia announced its plans to acquire Hugging Face, the U.S. Department of Justice began making inquiries about how the deal would impact competition in the AI market, Reuters reported in October . While Nvidia pledged that the platform would preserve open support, it would also allow the company to control a major distribution channel for AI models.
The Hugging Face deal is still scheduled to close in the first half of 2027. Requests for further comment on the deal status and whether Hugging Face has spoken yet with Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress were not returned.
Huang’s advocacy for open source and open-weight AI has long extended beyond Hugging Face. In July, the CEO published an AI policy letter as his first-ever post on the social network X . The letter, which was signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, Hugging Face, IBM, Palantir, and others, urged the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models. It said models that “anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure” are an important part of the AI ecosystem because they make AI “more accessible, adaptable, and widely available.”
Huang also wrote that open-weight models expand access to the AI economy, strengthen competition, and give customers greater control, as they know they won’t become locked into a single provider. “Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” his post on X stated.
For my first post, I’m sharing a letter @NVIDIA signed on why open models matter.
AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country.
Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty.… pic.twitter.com/t02bi51N4C — Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) July 24, 2026
In August, Nvidia also announced a $6 billion deal with the coding startup Poolside to help build out an open AI ecosystem in the U.S. to help the country compete against Chinese companies like DeepSeek and Kimi K3, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time. Last month, Nvidia expanded its Nemotron family of open-weight models with a large 120-billion-parameter model for agents used by the enterprise as well as with two new lightweight Bolt models that run on PCs.
Earlier this year, Huang promoted open source AI during his January keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, noting that open source models have “really revolutionized artificial intelligence.”

Nvidia Rival Fractile Hits $7B Valuation With $720M AI Chip Funding
British AI chip startup Fractile raises $720M at a $7B valuation, backed by Google, BlackRock and the UK government ahead of its 2027 chip launch.
Emir Abyazov 2 min read
12 November 2026, 01:14 PM Prefer us on Google
Key takeaways
Fractile raises $720 million at $7 billion valuation
Google and UK government back Nvidia challenger
First commercial AI chips expected in 2027
British AI chip startup Fractile has raised $720 million at a $7 billion valuation, attracting backing from Google-linked investors, BlackRock and the UK government as competition intensifies to develop alternatives to Nvidia's artificial intelligence processors.
The November 11 Series C round was co-led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint. Alphabet's CapitalG, DST Global, Balderton and several other investors also participated.
The UK government's announcement confirmed investments from its Sovereign AI fund and the British Business Bank, describing the financing as part of Britain's strategy to develop domestic semiconductor capabilities.
Fractile's $720M Funding Targets Nvidia's AI Chip Dominance
Founded in 2022 by Walter Goodwin, Fractile is developing processors specifically designed for AI inference, the process of generating responses after a model has been trained.
Unlike conventional AI accelerators, Fractile's architecture places dynamic random-access memory directly above processing components, seeking to reduce the delays caused by moving data between memory and computing units.
The company argues that memory bandwidth increasingly limits AI performance, particularly as reasoning models and autonomous agents generate longer outputs.
Its technology could eventually challenge Nvidia's dominant position in AI inference, although commercial performance remains unproven.
The financing arrives as Google expands its exposure to alternative AI chip developers, including a recently disclosed $548 million Qualcomm stake.
Other companies are pursuing similar opportunities through custom AI accelerators , as cloud providers seek more specialized computing hardware.
Google and UK Government Back Fractile's Expansion
Fractile's investors include major technology-focused funds alongside British public institutions, reflecting growing demand for alternatives to foreign semiconductor suppliers.
The British government said the investment would help the company expand its engineering operations across London and Bristol while strengthening domestic AI infrastructure.
The round also comes amid Nvidia's continued investment in AI chip research , where rapid innovation remains essential to protecting its competitive advantage.
However, Fractile faces significant execution challenges.
The company expects to introduce its first commercial chip in 2027, meaning its current valuation largely reflects investor expectations rather than established product revenue.
Can Fractile Challenge Nvidia in AI Inference?
Fractile is entering a competitive market that includes established semiconductor companies and emerging developers such as Groq and Etched.
Nvidia has already pursued inference technology investments to strengthen its position as AI workloads expand beyond model training.
Fractile must demonstrate that its architecture delivers meaningful improvements in speed, energy consumption and cost under real-world conditions.
Its financing also reflects the broader AI infrastructure investment boom , where substantial capital is flowing into companies before their technologies achieve commercial scale.

SoftBank Bets approximately $5.4 Billion on Swiss Robotics as Foreign Capital Influx Deepens
Add preferred source
Japan's SoftBank Group is pouring large sums into Switzerland's robotics industry, agreeing to acquire ABB's robotics division for $5.4 billion and investing $200 million in Gravis Robotics, a construction-robotics startup spun out of ETH Zurich. Foreign investors account for 88% of capital in deep-tech funding rounds of $100 million or more, and 43% of Swiss scale-ups are university or research-institute spin-offs. However, the share of Swiss investors in later-stage rounds has fallen from 27% to 13%, with limited mass-production experience and the flight of domestic capital cited as challenges at the growth stage.
Key Elements
SoftBank Group ABB Gravis Robotics ETH Zurich Deep Tech Nation Switzerland Switzerland Global Enterprise (S-GE) Neura Robotics Swissmem Swisscom Ventures EPFL
Japan's SoftBank Group is injecting large sums into Switzerland's robotics industry in quick succession. After agreeing to acquire the robotics division of Swiss automation company ABB for $5.4 billion (~7.2 trillion won), SoftBank in August invested $200 million (~270 billion won) in Gravis Robotics, a construction-robotics startup spun out of ETH Zurich. Gravis said the round was the largest Series A investment ever in the construction-robotics sector.
SoftBank's string of bets encapsulates the recent surge of foreign capital into Swiss deep-tech companies. According to the "Swiss Scale-up Report 2026" published this year by Deep Tech Nation Switzerland, foreign investors accounted for 88% of the capital in deep-tech funding rounds that raised $100 million or more. In effect, Swiss companies are raising their growth capital from abroad.
Speaking at a robotics and automation event hosted by Switzerland Global Enterprise (S-GE) in Zurich, Switzerland, on the 11th (local time), investment and industry officials agreed that foreign capital looks at the depth of research accumulated before a company's founding rather than its short history. They explained that technology and intellectual property (IP) built up over years in university labs, combined with research talent from around the world, heighten investment appeal.
Alexandre Meldem, head of international communications at Deep Tech Nation Switzerland, said, "Even if a company was only recently founded, there may be 10 years of science behind it," adding, "Switzerland is a relatively stable country with a predictable policy environment, which is an advantage because it allows investors to look 10 years ahead."
Indeed, research institutions are the key starting point for deep-tech companies in Switzerland. Of 265 Swiss scale-ups, 115—or 43%—are spin-offs from universities or research institutes. Forty-two came from ETH and 41 from EPFL. Some foreign robotics companies have even set up bases in Zurich directly to tap the research ecosystem. German robotics company Neura Robotics is developing core hardware technology for humanoid robots in Zurich.
Urs Laupi, chief strategy officer (CSO) of Neura Robotics, cited cooperation with ETH, physical AI research talent, and the capital environment as reasons for choosing Zurich as its base. "Switzerland has a solid knowledge base in the field of physical AI," he said, stressing that "we can combine world-class Swiss research capabilities with Germany's industrialization capabilities."
Switzerland also operates a separate intermediate stage to validate research results before they are applied on actual factory floors. The Swiss Cobotics Competence Center (S3C) at the Switzerland Innovation Park Biel/Bienne supports proof-of-concept (PoC) testing of robotics technology before companies invest in automation equipment, and once validation is complete, hands the results to system integrators and others to connect them to industrialization.
The competitiveness of Swiss robotics companies was not built on university research alone. As the precision machinery and automation industries developed long ago, a manufacturing base for applying lab technology to real industry was built alongside them. A Chinese venture capital (VC) official also cited precision machinery technology and the manufacturing base supporting it as reasons for paying attention to Swiss robotics companies.
Roger Sonderegger, industry sector manager at Swissmem, the Swiss association for the mechanical, electrical, and metal industries, explained that "high labor costs accelerated automation in Swiss manufacturing," adding that "from the 1970s and 1980s, automation was adopted to cope with high production costs, and competitiveness was built around precision machinery and high-value-added products rather than mass production."

LPL Financial Brings In $2.035 Billion In Combined Client Assets Represented By Four Joining Practices
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 4:03 PM
LPL Financial Brings In $2.035 Billion In Combined Client Assets Represented By Four Joining Practices
LPL Financial has welcomed four wealth management practices reporting approximately $2.035 billion in combined client assets, expanding its advisor network through affiliations announced over the last couple of days. SteadRock Private Wealth, FHT Advisors, Impel Wealth Management and Sound Foundation Wealth Advisors joined LPL’s broker-dealer and Registered Investment Advisor platforms. The reported assets include advisory, brokerage and retirement plan assets.
SteadRock Private Wealth
Nathan J. “Nate” Hershman joined LPL from Edward Jones to launch SteadRock Private Wealth in North Canton, Ohio. He reported serving approximately $185 million in advisory, brokerage and retirement plan assets.
SteadRock serves families, individuals approaching or living in retirement, and business owners, including those in manufacturing. Its planning approach connects investments and retirement needs with business interests, charitable priorities and financial legacies.
For business owners, planning can include preparing for a transition and evaluating how a sale or succession could affect retirement and family objectives. Hershman selected LPL to establish an independent practice with access to its technology, investment platform and business support.
FHT Advisors
FHT Advisors joined LPL from Cetera alongside Impel Wealth Management. The two Ohio-based practices reported approximately $1.15 billion in combined client assets and will retain their separate identities.
Led by Brian Toma, FHT serves clients across 32 states, including professionals, medical professionals, younger families, people approaching retirement and retirees.
The firm operates as an ensemble practice, bringing multiple advisors’ experience and planning perspectives to client relationships. Its advisory team includes Sarah Stewart, Tom Drager, Tammy Hafner, Bruce Baker, Bear Rupert, Jonathan Goldston, Seann Schaller and financial consultant Stephen Ehrhardt.
FHT identified LPL’s technology, planning capabilities and resources as factors supporting its next stage of development.
Impel Wealth Management
Jesse Hurst leads Impel Wealth Management, which began by serving corporate executives around Akron and has expanded into multigenerational wealth management.
Hurst works alongside advisors Nathan Ollish and Irene Zurowski. Ollish serves many next-generation clients, while Zurowski’s focus includes retirement plans and female executives.
Impel works with dozens of families across at least two generations and more than a dozen across three generations. The team also produces market and financial planning commentary through recurring blog posts and videos.
Hurst and FHT’s Toma have worked alongside one another for 25 years, exchanging ideas and best practices while independently leading their firms. Impel selected LPL for its technology, advanced planning resources and growth opportunities.
Sound Foundation Wealth Advisors
Sound Foundation Wealth Advisors joined from Cambridge Investment Research Advisors, reporting approximately $700 million in advisory, brokerage and retirement plan assets.
Founded by Nathan Downs and Cory Thomas, the Boise, Idaho-headquartered practice traces its beginnings to 2018. It has developed shared operations and business processes to support a nationwide advisory team.
Its advisors also include Seth Church, Cameron Church, Caleb Whalen, Kason Wedel, Dustin Olson and Cory McLeaf.
Sound Foundation serves clients including technology, healthcare and higher education professionals, as well as business owners. Its planning process starts with each household’s income, expenses, assets and objectives before developing individualized recommendations.
The founders cited LPL’s investment in technology and systems, along with its ability to support the practice’s evolving needs, as reasons for joining.
LPL supports more than 32,000 financial advisors and the wealth management practices of approximately 1,100 financial institutions. It services and custodies approximately $2.6 trillion in brokerage and advisory assets on behalf of approximately 8 million Americans.

candidates.title: With $720M round, Britain’s Fractile gets a leg up in the race for AI chips
candidates.snippet: With $720M round, Britain’s Fractile gets a leg up in the race for AI chips TechCrunch
candidates.text:
Fractile , a British startup developing AI chips, has raised a $720 million Series C backed by Britain’s Sovereign AI Fund with hopes of “ensuring the U.K. has a greater stake in the hardware that will underpin its future economy,” its government stated .
Alongside the likes of Axelera , Etched , and OLIX , this makes Fractile one of the top-funded startup players in the race for purpose-built AI chips. Such chips are one of several avenues being explored to reduce the cost of inference — aka using increasingly demanding AI models in production.
However, Fractile seeks to go beyond hardware with a full-stack approach that also includes a machine learning compiler to maximize the speed at which LLMs will get executed on its chips.
As a result, the company frames itself as a frontier AI company, and its latest round led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Redpoint was priced accordingly. According to the British government, the valuation was “over £5 billion” — quite possibly $7 billion, a figure reported both by the Financial Times and a Reuters source .
Still, Fractile’s main differentiator will arguably be its hardware design. After a pivot , its approach now revolves on DRAM, the most common type of RAM, but stacked on top of each chip in such a way that it is hoping will bypass the usual trade-off between memory and capacity.
This trade-off has become more problematic with the rise of agentic AI, as companies seek to perform longer chains of tasks with large models without compromising on speed. As compute struggles to keep up, hopes are high for AI chips, despite their limited availability to date.
In a LinkedIn post , Fractile CEO Walter Goodwin wrote that “there is still a lot of work ahead” for the company, and that the new funding will enable the startup to “ship [its] first chips and systems next year.”

candidates.snippet: SoftBank-Led Agile Robots Raises $500M Series F at $8.5B Valuation Wowtale
candidates.text:
A German company that has deployed more than 20,000 industrial robot solutions now has a plant that can build up to 10,000 humanoids a year. Munich-based Physical AI company Agile Robots has raised a $500 million Series F led by SoftBank Group, valuing it at $8.5 billion and bringing total funding to $2 billion.
Agile Robots announced the round on Nov. 12. SoftBank Group led, with NVIDIA, Hitachi Group (Hitachi and Hitachi Ventures) and T.Capital among the participants. The company says the investors span the automotive, artificial intelligence, digital and industrial technology sectors. SoftBank is a longtime backer: its Vision Fund 2 led the company’s $220 million Series C in September 2021 at a valuation above $1 billion, so the new valuation is more than eight times that. According to Bloomberg, a round of about $800 million, with SoftBank anchoring more than $300 million, was under discussion in June, and the round closed smaller at $500 million. Hitachi Ventures also joined Graphon Labs’ $35 million Series A this month.
The company builds humanoid and mobile robots, robotic arms and hands, and the software and AI models behind them, aimed at automotive, consumer electronics, healthcare and service customers that want to automate tasks that have relied on human dexterity and judgment. It was founded in 2018 as a spin-off from the German Aerospace Center (DLR) and says it has deployed 20,000 industrial robotic solutions across automotive, consumer electronics, logistics and other industries. It has more than 3,500 employees from almost 60 countries, including more than 2,000 R&D experts, and over 650 patents, and develops and builds its hardware and software in-house from more than 20,000 square meters of lab space.
Founder and CEO Zhaopeng Chen said the company wants to bring Physical AI out of the lab and into industrial production across logistics, automotive, electronics and manufacturing. The money will go to global expansion, a stronger presence in key markets and more production capacity. Agile Robots plans to strengthen its presence in the United States and speed up development of new robotics applications, while continuing to build out production capacity, including in Germany. A new site opened early this year in Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich, can produce up to 10,000 legged and wheeled humanoid robots a year. Dennis Chang, managing partner at SoftBank Investment Advisers, said Agile Robots combines deep robotics expertise with the ability to execute at industrial scale, and that SoftBank looks forward to continuing to partner with Chen’s team.
Acquisitions have widened the business. In November 2023 it took over the operations of insolvent Munich robotics company Franka Emika , which now runs as Franka Robotics and serves as an AI robotics research platform. Last November it announced the acquisition of thyssenkrupp’s Automation Engineering business , and in April it closed the deal . The unit now operates as industrial deployment specialist Krause Automation, and the company said at the time it would add about 650 experts and 10 locations in Europe and North America. BÄR Automation and Idealworks are also subsidiaries, and its humanoid lineup includes Agile ONE. The company has not disclosed revenue.
Humanoid competition is heating up on both sides of the Atlantic. The closest comparison is fellow German company NEURA Robotics , based in Metzingen, which also builds the full stack from cobot arms and mobile platforms to its 4NE1 humanoid and the Neuraverse platform. In June it announced a Series C of up to $1.4 billion led by Tether at a reported valuation of about $7 billion, with the full amount contingent on performance milestones, a different structure from Agile Robots’ $500 million. In the US, Figure AI is valued at $39 billion and has tested its robots at a BMW plant, and Apptronik , partnered with Google DeepMind, raised $935 million in a Series A alone at a $5.3 billion valuation. Agility Robotics has built more than $300 million in multiyear contracts by renting robots to warehouses as a service and is going public through a SPAC merger at a $2.5 billion valuation. While those companies lean first on AI models or specific sites, Agile Robots starts from the manufacturing and delivery experience of 20,000 deployed industrial robot solutions.

By: Asia Business Outlook Team | Thursday, 12 November 2026
Japanese investment group SoftBank has led a US$500 million funding round in German robotics company Agile Robots , valuing the company at US$8.5 billion.
The funding round also saw participation from semiconductor company Nvidia , Japanese technology firm Hitachi and T. Capital.
The investment comes as interest in artificial intelligence and robotics continues to grow, with more companies looking to use these technologies in manufacturing and other industries.
Agile Robots plans to use the funds to expand its business in the United States, increase production in Germany and develop new industrial applications.
The company is looking to benefit from the growing demand for automation technology across manufacturing, logistics and other sectors. The investment is also expected to help it strengthen its position in the global robotics market .
Key Highlights
SoftBank Leads $500 Million Funding Round in German Robotics Firm Agile Robots
Agile Robots Reaches $8.5 Billion Valuation After SoftBank-Led Investment
Nvidia and Hitachi Join SoftBank in $500 Million Investment in Agile Robots
SoftBank and Nvidia Support Agile Robots' Expansion
Founded in 2018 by researchers from the German Aerospace Center, Agile Robots develops robotic systems that combine artificial intelligence with advanced hardware. Its products include industrial robotic arms , robotic hands, autonomous transport systems and humanoid robots used for different industrial applications.
The company has more than 3,500 employees across over 25 locations worldwide. It also says that more than 20,000 of its automation solutions are currently in use globally. Agile Robots holds over 650 patents related to its technology.
With the latest investment, the company has raised approximately US$2 billion since its establishment. SoftBank had previously led a US$220 million Series C funding round in Agile Robots in 2021, helping it expand its operations.
Nvidia's participation is another important part of the deal. The chipmaker has been increasing its investments and partnerships in robotics as it looks to expand the use of AI beyond computers and data centres. This includes physical AI , which allows machines to understand their surroundings and carry out tasks in the real world.
Agile Robots has also partnered with Google DeepMind to improve the capabilities of its robotic systems. The collaboration is aimed at developing robots that can perform more complex tasks in industrial settings.
Company Plans to Increase Production in Germany
Agile Robots will use the new funding to expand its operations in the United States and increase its manufacturing capacity in Germany. It also plans to develop more applications for its robotic systems as manufacturers look for ways to improve productivity and reduce manual work.
Earlier this year, the company opened a manufacturing facility in Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich. The facility is designed to produce up to 10,000 humanoid robots annually. This will help Agile Robots increase production and prepare for growing demand.
The company sees humanoid robots as an important part of the future of industrial automation . Designed to work in spaces built for humans, these robots could be used in factories, warehouses and other workplaces to handle different tasks.
The investment also reflects SoftBank's growing interest in artificial intelligence and robotics. The Japanese group has been backing companies developing technologies that combine AI software with physical machines. Its agreement to acquire ABB's robotics division for US$5.4 billion is another example of its interest in the sector.

Peak 10 Energy: $500 Million Facility To Finance Oil And Gas Acquisitions
Peak 10 Energy has established a financing partnership with U.S. Bank that provides as much as $500 million for acquisitions of producing oil and gas assets across the U.S.
The acquisition finance facility will support Peak 10’s strategy of consolidating packages weighted toward proved developed producing properties. These assets have established production and can generate more predictable cash flows than undeveloped acreage.
U.S. Bank structured the facility to support later asset-backed securities issuances. That approach could provide longer-term institutional financing after Peak 10 completes and assembles acquisitions.
Peak 10 was founded in 2023 and has completed 12 acquisition and divestiture transactions involving operated properties, non-operated interests, and mineral assets across U.S. onshore basins.
The new facility will allow the company to pursue larger transactions and close acquisitions more quickly. Peak 10 said it encountered additional opportunities during 2026 that it could have acquired if the facility had already been available.
The company also maintains a commodity hedging relationship with U.S. Bank. Hedging can help stabilize cash flow from acquired properties and support financing by reducing exposure to oil and gas price volatility.
Peak 10’s strategy focuses on extending the productive lives of existing fields and infrastructure. The company expects this approach to support domestic energy production without depending solely on new exploration.
Legacy Star Capital Partners backs Peak 10 and views the combination of producing-asset consolidation and asset-backed financing as a long-duration investment strategy.
Petrie Partners originated the transaction and advised Peak 10. Baker Botts served as Peak 10’s legal adviser, while Haynes Boone represented U.S. Bank.

At launch, the fund has already secured its first two storage projects in central Germany under purchase agreements and has an identified project pipeline representing an investment volume of more than €300 million.
As renewable energy deployment progresses, large-scale battery storage systems are becoming an important component in stabilizing the German electricity grid and balancing volatile generation peaks. The IIBF translates this structural infrastructure need into an investment profile tailored to regulated institutional investors: the fund invests in a diversified portfolio of large-scale battery storage projects in Germany that are ready to build or close to their commercial operation date (COD) and holds them for the long term following acquisition. Early-stage project development and permitting risks therefore remain outside the fund.
Clearly defined responsibilities: institutional investment management and European energy trading expertise
The IIBF is built on a clearly defined division of responsibilities between two established specialists in their respective markets:
Investment management, underwriting and structuring by 2IP: Institutional Investment Partners (2IP) is responsible for investment management, transaction underwriting and institutional fund structuring. Market access, asset management, software and energy trading by Second Foundation: As one of Europe's major technology-driven energy traders, the Second Foundation Group manages the energy-related and technological value chain surrounding the storage facilities. Contractually underpinned base distributions with additional market upside
The IIBF's income model is designed to cushion downside exposure to the volatility typical of electricity markets while also harnessing it for the portfolio. The core of the fund's income consists of long-term contractual usage fees (lease payments) for making the storage facilities available. Contractual advance payments and additional security mechanisms support the predictability of regular distributions to investors.
In addition, performance-linked remuneration components allow investors to participate directly in Second Foundation's trading performance in the electricity and balancing markets. Zacua Ventures Raises $135 Million to Invest in AI, Robotics and Industrial Technology
Published on: 11 November، 2026
Zacua Ventures
Zacua Ventures closes its $135 million Fund II to back Physical AI, construction robotics, industrial technology, energy, manufacturing and infrastructure startups.
The next major opportunity in artificial intelligence may not be confined to software applications or foundation models.
Increasingly, investors are looking toward technologies that can transform the physical economy, from construction sites and cement factories to energy networks, manufacturing facilities and data centers.
Zacua Ventures is positioning itself at the center of this shift, closing its second fund at $135 million to expand investments beyond construction technology into a broader range of Physical Industries, including robotics, manufacturing, energy, mining and critical infrastructure.
$135 Million to Back Technologies Building the Physical Economy
Zacua Ventures closed Fund II at $135 million, more than doubling its $56 million debut fund and exceeding its fundraising target by 35%.
The raise reflects growing investor interest in technology applied to capital-intensive industries that have historically attracted less venture capital than software and digital platforms.
The firm’s investment thesis is built around a simple premise: construction, energy, manufacturing and mining are not merely facing productivity challenges.
They need fundamental operational transformation through AI, robotics, data and advanced technologies.
AI Is Moving From Digital Applications to Physical Industries
Zacua’s strategy extends beyond conventional AI tools, targeting companies that deploy technology directly into industrial and field operations.
Its investments include autonomous construction robots, AI platforms that identify project risks before construction begins, and technologies designed to reduce emissions from cement production.
These businesses are becoming increasingly relevant as industries face labor shortages, aging workforces, complex operational processes and growing demand for AI infrastructure.
The opportunity is not simply to automate existing workflows, but to redesign how physical industries operate.
Why Venture Capital Is Turning Toward Physical Industries
Construction, energy, manufacturing and mining represent enormous markets with persistent productivity gaps and substantial infrastructure requirements.
McKinsey estimates that global infrastructure investment needs will reach $106 trillion through 2040, while Gartner projects data-center power demand could reach 290 gigawatts by 2030.
These requirements create opportunities for startups developing technologies that improve industrial productivity, reduce operating costs and reshape supply chains.
However, investing in physical industries is fundamentally different from funding software companies. Technologies must be tested in real operating environments, integrated into existing equipment and workflows, and demonstrate measurable economic value before they can scale.
From Construction Robotics to Low-Carbon Cement
Zacua’s early Fund II investments illustrate the breadth of its strategy.
Origin Robotics develops autonomous robots capable of finishing interior walls, while CURA Climate is working to electrify cement production and reduce emissions by up to 85% through its pilot technology.
Neuron Factory applies AI to preconstruction planning, using a proprietary knowledge graph to identify risks and coordinate project decisions.
These companies highlight an important investment principle: the value of industrial technology depends not only on innovation, but also on its ability to solve expensive operational problems in markets where implementation can be challenging.
Corporate Networks Give Zacua a Commercialization Advantage
Zacua is backed by more than 30 corporate and institutional investors across over 20 countries, including Volvo Group Venture Capital, Holcim Maqer Ventures, Hilti Venture, Trimble Ventures and Dubai Future District Fund.
The network provides startups with access to industrial customers, strategic partners and real-world operating environments.
This support can help founders overcome one of the most difficult barriers in industrial technology: moving from a promising prototype to commercially deployed solutions at scale.
The Real Investment Opportunity Is Industrial Productivity
Zacua Ventures represents a growing venture-capital thesis that treats technology as a tool for rebuilding the physical economy rather than simply creating another generation of digital applications.
As AI investment expands into construction, energy, manufacturing and mining, startups capable of delivering measurable productivity improvements could become major beneficiaries of the next investment cycle.
The challenge remains execution.
Industrial startups must demonstrate economic value, secure customer adoption and manage complex deployment requirements before their technologies can generate sustainable returns.
For venture capital, the opportunity may be substantial—but the winners will be those that turn advanced technology into measurable improvements in the real world.

Mavria was founded by former colleagues from the U.S. Department of Energy. Co-founders Nick Poradek and Adam Blake previously served as senior advisors to the U.S. Secretary of Energy, while Co-founder Seth Cohen was a former head of nuclear law and policy.
Adam Blake, Mavria's CEO, noted that the race in intelligence is moving from the lab into the physical world. He stated that intelligence needs data centers, which require power, factories, equipment, supply chains, and skilled workers. Blake highlighted that much of this infrastructure is currently built one custom project at a time, with timelines measured in years.
Mavria's approach focuses on producing infrastructure through standardized manufacturing. This aims to move away from individually designed construction projects, which can be time-consuming. The company's launch coincides with increasing demand for electricity, data centers, and industrial equipment due to the expansion of AI computing capacity. Geneva, Switzerland, November 11, 2026 - Addex Therapeutics (SIX and Nasdaq: ADXN), a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on developing a portfolio of novel small molecule allosteric modulators for neurological disorders, today announced that its spin-out company, Neurosterix, has closed a $105 million Series B financing from a syndicate of leading life science investors. Addex did not participate in the financing and its equity interest now represents 8.5% of the issued capital at a valuation of $18.6 million.
The proceeds raised will support mainly the planned Phase 2 clinical development of NTX-253, a highly selective muscarinic M4 positive allosteric modulator (PAM), for schizophrenia. The financing will also support Neurosterix’s broader pipeline of selective allosteric modulators for a range of neuropsychiatric disorders.
“The closing of this significant financing is a huge endorsement of the allosteric approach pioneered by Addex in schizophrenia as well as other neuropsychiatric disorders. Congatulations to the whole Neurosterix team, which has made enormous strides in advancing lead program NTX-253 through clinical development and ready for Phase 2, following our spin-out in 2024,” said Tim Dyer, CEO of Addex.
About NTX-253 and M4 PAMs
The M4 muscarinic receptor is a validated target for treating schizophrenia and related disorders through indirect modulation of dopamine signaling. NTX-253 is a potent, highly selective, oral PAM of M4 that fine-tunes muscarinic signaling in the brain to potentially reduce psychosis symptoms while avoiding the movement disorders and metabolic complications associated with traditional dopamine antagonists. Neurosterix has completed Phase 1 single- and multiple-ascending-dose clinical studies of NTX-253, which data supporting advancing into larger scale Phase 2 clinical studies.
About Neurosterix
Neurosterix is a clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on transforming neuropsychiatric care through selective allosteric modulation. The company’s approach is designed to fine-tune brain signaling with greater precision and selectivity, with the goal of developing safer, more effective treatments for people living with schizophrenia, and mood and anxiety disorders. Neurosterix’s pipeline includes NTX-253, a selective muscarinic M4 positive allosteric modulator (PAM) for schizophrenia; NTX-819, a potentially first-in-class mGlu7 negative allosteric modulator (NAM) for mood and anxiety disorders; and NTX-529, a second differentiated M4 PAM for additional psychosis- and mood-related disorders. Neurosterix has operations in Boston and Geneva. For more information, visit www.neurosterix.com.
About Addex Therapeutics
Addex Therapeutics is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on developing a portfolio of novel small molecule allosteric modulators for neurological disorders. Addex's lead drug candidate, dipraglurant (mGlu5 negative allosteric modulator or NAM), is under evaluation for future development in brain injury recovery, including post-stroke and traumatic brain injury recovery. Addex has selected a GABAB PAM drug candidate for development in substance use disorders and has successfully completed IND enabling studies. In addition, Addex is advancing a differentiated GABAB PAM compound for the treatment of chronic cough. Addex holds a 8.5% equity interest in a private spin out company, Neurosterix US Holdings LLC, which is advancing a portfolio of allosteric modulator programs, including M4 PAM for schizophrenia, psychosis and mood-related disorders and mGlu7 NAM for mood disorders. Addex has also invested in Stalicla, a private Swiss company pioneering a precision medicine approach for neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders.

Enza Capital is raising up to $80 Million to bet on African AI Startups
0
By
Smart Megwai
on
November 11, 2026
Africa , Business , Funding , Investments , Startups
Enza Capital has secured a first close of $21 million for its third fund, Enza Capital III LP, which it will dedicate entirely to artificial-intelligence startups across Africa.
The pan-African venture firm, which has offices in Nairobi, Johannesburg and Cairo, is targeting $60 million for the fund with a hard cap of $80 million, and expects a final close in about a year, the firm said in an emailed statement .
The fund’s entire thesis rests on a gap. African AI, by the report’s account, attracts relatively little venture capital despite growing interest in its potential. Investors deployed about $46.8 million into African AI startups through 2026, the report says, concentrated mostly in fintech and risk-intelligence companies and modest next to AI investment in other regions.
A Briter Bridges report cited in the report found that 30% of surveyed African AI companies are entirely bootstrapped, with funding clustered among more established players; some founders say investors’ preference for proven traction makes it harder for early-stage AI companies to raise money at all.
Enza Capital is betting that the gap in African AI funding is a market failure to be exploited, not a verdict on the sector’s potential.
Enza Capital’s existing investments span SeamlessHR, Money254, Sendy, Gigmile and Peach Payments, giving a sense of the firm’s range before this fund narrows its focus specifically to AI.
That earlier spread, across HR tech, personal finance, logistics and payments, suggests Enza Capital III LP will be looking for AI applied across similarly varied sectors rather than betting narrowly on one vertical.
What to watch
The first thing to consider is the pace over the next 12 months. To move from a target of $21 million to a goal of $60 million, and even aiming for a hard cap of $80 million, it will be essential to convince limited partners that the funding gap in African AI is investable rather than simply an indicator that the market has already assessed the associated risks.
The second point to consider is whether the fund’s eventual portfolio will focus primarily on fintech and risk-intelligence companies, which have already attracted most of the continent’s AI capital, or if it will genuinely explore newer categories that the report indicates are currently underfunded and lacking institutional investment.

Alta: $80 Million In Total Funding Advances Institutional Blockchain Infrastructure
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 6:38 PM
Alta: $80 Million In Total Funding Advances Institutional Blockchain Infrastructure
Alta has raised $80 million in total funding, including a $47.5 million Series A led by Index Ventures, to develop blockchain infrastructure designed for regulated financial institutions. GV, Blackbird Ventures, Square Peg and Capital 49 participated in the Series A. The total also includes $32.5 million in previous seed financing.
Alta is building infrastructure that allows financial assets and products to move globally and programmatically, with privacy, compliance, identity and authorization controls incorporated into the blockchain itself.
Its architecture uses recursive zero-knowledge cryptography to verify that transactions meet required rules while keeping balances, transaction details, identities and compliance policies private. The company intends the system to support activity across assets, blockchain networks and jurisdictions.
Airwallex has selected Alta as a technology partner, connecting its global payments infrastructure with Alta’s blockchain. The collaboration will support stablecoin pay-ins and payouts, alongside connectivity to local fiat payment networks across 200 countries and 90 currencies.
Alta positions its infrastructure as a neutral foundation that banks, payment providers and other financial institutions can use to develop services.
Its first product will focus on corporate liquidity management. Built around tokenized assets, the offering is intended to enable just-in-time funding, improve foreign exchange efficiency and reduce the cash businesses keep in prefunded accounts.
The product will also allow businesses to move into and out of yield-bearing tokenized assets, helping them earn interest on capital that would otherwise remain idle. Alta cited an estimated $4 trillion held in prefunded accounts globally as evidence of the opportunity to improve capital efficiency.
The company’s founders include CEO Loong Wang, President Catherine Porter and Airwallex Co-Founder and CEO Jack Zhang. They identified institutional controls and connectivity as requirements for expanding blockchain-based finance, including transactions initiated by AI agents.
Alta will use the funding to continue developing its blockchain, expand institutional partnerships and global financial connectivity, and grow its engineering and compliance teams.
KEY QUOTES
“Existing blockchains aren’t designed for the privacy and compliance requirements of global financial institutions. We’re taking a fundamentally different approach, building privacy, programmable compliance, and identity and authorization directly into the blockchain. This will enable money and assets to move instantly, globally, and securely, whether it’s a bank settling a transaction or an AI agent making a payment.”
Loong Wang, Co-Founder And CEO Of Alta
“Technology alone won’t be enough to modernize global finance. Financial institutions need infrastructure they can trust, with clear controls over who they’re transacting with, where money can move, and how sensitive information is protected. As AI agents increasingly make financial decisions and execute transactions, that trust becomes even more critical. Privacy, compliance, and accountability just aren’t barriers to innovation – they’re what will allow it to scale.”
Catherine Porter, Co-Founder And President Of Alta
“With the rise of agentic banking and programmable payments, stablecoins are becoming an important vector for settlement. Financial institutions need blockchain infrastructure that is private, neutral, regulated, and connected to global fiat rails. Alta is building exactly that. We’re proud to be an early design partner and help Alta deliver onchain finance at institutional scale.”
Jack Zhang, Co-Founder Of Alta And Co-Founder And CEO Of Airwallex
“Loong is the sort of technologist you only meet a few times in a career. After a major fintech exit from his first company, he went on to run the largest supercomputing calculation in history at its time, then discovered a cancer drug now in human trials. With Catherine’s exceptional track record of bringing industry leaders to the table and Jack’s understanding of the problem space, this is a team we had to back.”

Eli Radiopharma: Nearly $60 Million Series A Financing To Advance Radiopharmaceutical Pipeline Toward Clinical Development
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 11:27 AM
Eli Radiopharma: Nearly $60 Million Series A Financing To Advance Radiopharmaceutical Pipeline Toward Clinical Development
Eli Radiopharma has raised nearly $60 million (RMB 400 million) in Series A financing to advance its radiopharmaceutical pipeline toward clinical development. The funding will support preclinical research, regulatory submissions, early-stage clinical studies, and the expansion of the company’s research and development capabilities.
Huagai Capital led the financing round, with Bayland Capital serving as co-lead investor. Additional participants included Boyu Ventures, Delian Capital, InnoPinnacle Fund, Haibang Venture, Bairui Capital, Shenzhen Angel FOF Management, and Grand Flight Investment.
Existing shareholders CSPC & Growth Bio Fund, Huaige Capital, KHK Fund, Longfeng Venture, Hongsheng Capital, Bioclub Fund, and Skyfield Capital also participated in the financing.
Eli Radiopharma plans to allocate the proceeds toward preclinical research, investigational new drug applications, and early-stage clinical development. The company will also strengthen its research platforms, recruit additional talent, expand clinical operations, and pursue business development opportunities.
Founded in 2024, Eli Radiopharma focuses on developing radiopharmaceutical products that combine molecular targeting with radionuclide technology. Its pipeline includes diagnostic and therapeutic candidates designed to address unmet medical needs in oncology and neurological diseases.
The company has advanced multiple programs targeting novel molecular mechanisms through lead discovery, laboratory validation, and animal studies. Several candidates are approaching investigational new drug submissions, representing an important transition from early research toward human clinical testing.
Radiopharmaceuticals combine targeting molecules with radioactive isotopes to identify or treat diseased tissue. Therapeutic radioligands are designed to deliver radiation directly to tumors while limiting exposure to surrounding healthy tissue. Related diagnostic imaging agents can help physicians identify appropriate patients, evaluate disease progression, and monitor treatment responses.
The financing also reflects growing international interest in radiopharmaceutical innovation originating in China. Global pharmaceutical companies have increasingly explored opportunities involving novel molecular targets, therapeutic radionuclides, and expanded clinical applications.
Eli Radiopharma’s investors identified these areas as important drivers of future industry growth, particularly as radiopharmaceutical technologies move into additional cancer indications and other therapeutic applications.
The company’s longer-term strategy includes building a globally competitive pipeline capable of serving patients in international markets, including the U.S. and Europe. Its immediate priorities involve completing preclinical development, meeting regulatory requirements, and advancing differentiated candidates into clinical studies.
The Series A financing provides Eli Radiopharma with additional resources to move its lead programs closer to clinical validation while expanding the infrastructure needed to support a broader radiopharmaceutical development portfolio.

Bay Raises $50 Million to Stop AI Agents From Making Dangerous Decisions Inside Companies
Epil Bodra
| November 11 | Business Stories , Funding Feed
Share
Cybersecurity startup Bay has emerged from stealth with $50 million in funding , just nine months after its founding, as businesses face growing security risks from autonomous AI agents operating across corporate systems.
The company, founded in early 2026 by former Israeli intelligence and cybersecurity professionals, has developed technology designed to detect and block potentially harmful actions by AI agents, including those operating with legitimate access permissions.
The funding includes a $37 million Series A led by Battery Ventures , with participation from Micron Ventures, Microsoft’s venture capital arm M12, and Wiz CEO Assaf Rappaport. Bay also disclosed an earlier $13 million seed round backed by YL Ventures and Striker.
Cisco Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel and former Zscaler Chief Strategy Officer Manoj Apte are among the company’s private investors.
Bay was established by CEO Yuval Zacharia, Chief Product Officer Aner Morag , and Vice President of Research and Development Boris Danilovich.
The founders identified a critical security problem after one of their own AI coding agents attempted to expose a cloud environment to the public internet while completing a test.
The agent had not been compromised, nor was it acting under instructions from an attacker. Instead, it was using authorized permissions to accomplish its assigned task, potentially creating a serious security vulnerability in the process.
That experience became the foundation for Bay’s approach to AI security, which focuses on preventing dangerous actions even when an agent is functioning as intended.
Unlike traditional security systems that primarily focus on unauthorized access or malicious activity, Bay examines what an AI agent is attempting to accomplish and whether its actions could violate an organization’s security policies.
Its platform discovers AI agents operating across corporate environments and analyzes their activities within the context of an entire session, including their assigned objectives and previous actions.
Based on that information, the system can approve an action, block it, or refer it for human authorization. Bay says these decisions occur locally within milliseconds, allowing permitted operations to continue without disrupting workflows.
The technology supports AI assistants, coding agents, custom-built agents, and the tools they use across employee devices, cloud infrastructure, and software-as-a-service applications.
Bay also claims its platform can be deployed in under five minutes using existing corporate security infrastructure, without installing additional persistent endpoint agents or network proxies.
The company says its technology is already being used by dozens of enterprise customers across finance, insurance, manufacturing, media, and technology.
Wix, ClickUp, Micron, and Peloton are among its named customers. Micron is also participating in the company’s latest funding round through Micron Ventures.
Zacharia told Calcalist that Bay’s rapid fundraising was supported by early customer demand and revenue growth. She said the company generated millions in revenue during its first quarter of sales, although an exact figure was not disclosed.
“We raised a significant amount of capital, and we did so very quickly. The primary driver was the large number of customers we managed to acquire and the revenue we generated in such a short timeframe, which helped us close the funding round rapidly,” Zacharia said.
The startup currently employs approximately 35 people, primarily in Israel, and plans to expand its product development and engineering operations.
It also intends to strengthen its sales, marketing, and customer-facing teams in the United States and Europe, with Zacharia planning to relocate to the US.
Bay’s leadership brings experience from Israeli military intelligence and major cybersecurity companies.
Zacharia previously served in Unit 8200 before becoming director of research and AI at Hunters. Morag also worked in Unit 8200 and later became vice president of product at Noname Security.
Danilovich previously worked at Preempt Security and subsequently held senior engineering leadership roles at CrowdStrike, where he managed a department of approximately 90 engineers.
With its latest funding, Bay plans to accelerate product development and expand adoption among enterprises deploying autonomous AI systems.
The company’s central challenge is one that traditional access controls alone cannot necessarily resolve: an AI agent may have permission to perform an action, but that does not mean the action is safe.
As organizations give AI systems greater autonomy, Bay is positioning its technology to assess those actions before they create security problems.

candidates.title: Graphon Labs Raises $35M Series A to Give AI Agents Long-Term Memory
candidates.snippet: Graphon Labs Raises $35M Series A to Give AI Agents Long-Term Memory Wowtale
candidates.text:
AI models keep getting smarter, yet they still struggle to understand the videos, documents and conversations people have accumulated. A startup building memory infrastructure that preserves the structure of that data has now raised a Series A.
Graphon Labs announced a $35 million Series A on Nov. 10. RRE Ventures led the round, and according to the press release, HP, Energy Impact Partners, Hitachi Ventures and Gaia VC participated. It comes six months after the company’s seed round and brings total funding to $43.3 million. Graphon plans to use the money to expand its infrastructure for developers and enterprise customers, then extend from the cloud and on-premises deployments to consumer devices.
The seed round drew some attention in Korea. According to May reports from The Next Web and SiliconAngle, Novera Ventures led the $8.3 million seed, with Perplexity Fund, Hitachi Ventures, Gaia Ventures, Samsung Next and GS Futures also participating. The Next Web reported that GS Group is an early customer, using the technology for convenience-store traffic analysis and safety monitoring on construction sites.
The problem Graphon targets is that AI “memory” today is mostly storage. Fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) have been used to bring company knowledge into models, but when documents are cut into pieces and searched as vectors, sentences with nearly identical words and opposite meanings, such as “refund allowed” and “refund not allowed,” can land close together. A rule may be found while the fragment holding its exception is missed. The company likens it to tearing a book apart page by page, crumpling the pages and trying to find them again.
Its answer is to keep the structure. Graphon reads mixed data such as video, images, spreadsheets, recordings and markdown files and builds a detailed graph without deciding in advance which relationships will matter. It then uses a compressed representation of that graph, the “graphon,” to guide where to search. According to press reports, the graphon is a mathematical concept formalized around 2008 by UC Berkeley professors Jennifer Chayes and Christian Borgs, among others, and the two serve as technical advisers.
Developers use it much like S3: put files in a bucket and Graphon builds the structure. The website lists four APIs, Storage, Search, Answer and Research. Products are split into Graphon Enterprise, Graphon Developer and Graphon On-Device Memory for phones, laptops, cameras and wearables, and enterprise customers can choose hosted, customer-managed VPC or on-premises deployment.
The performance figures are the company’s own. Graphon says it scored 93.9% accuracy on the LoCoMo conversational memory benchmark while using 58% fewer tokens than loading the full conversation, and 90.2% accuracy with 95% token savings on ConvoMem. On ATM-Bench, which spans video, audio and text, it reported 81.7%, 5.0 percentage points ahead of the next entry on the public leaderboard. None of these numbers has been independently verified.
Disclosed customers include the San Francisco 49ers and Hitachi Rail. The 49ers are weighing it for finding sponsorship opportunities and supporting staff work, while Hitachi Rail is evaluating its potential to surface contextual knowledge in industrial settings and improve AI reasoning. RRE Ventures’ Raju Rishi pointed to the fact that models can reason and agents can act, yet neither improves without accumulating knowledge, as the reason for investing.
The company is led by CEO Arbaaz Khan , who said in the company blog that working as an applied scientist on an Amazon customer service team made him feel the gap between a plausible answer and a correct one. He founded the company with Clark, with whom he had researched graph-based techniques since their PhD days to help robots remember where they had been and explore unfamiliar environments. May reports named Clark Zhang as chief technology officer and Deepak Mishra as chief operating officer. The company says its team includes engineers and researchers from Amazon, Meta, Google, Apple and NVIDIA.
Several startups are already competing in the agent memory layer. Mem0 lets developers add persistent memory to AI with a few lines of code and has raised $24 million across its seed and Series A. Supermemory , founded by a 19-year-old, raised a $3 million seed for a memory engine that analyzes documents, chats and emails. Memories.ai focuses on video memory, processing up to 10 million hours of footage, and raised an $8 million seed with Samsung Next participating. Letta , backed by Felicis, is also named as a rival. While those companies lean toward particular kinds of data such as conversation logs or video, Graphon pitches weaving video, documents and spreadsheets into a single graph.

Dreeze Emerges From Stealth With $33M to Rebuild Cloud Apps After Cyberattacks
Created by Zerto and Kashya veterans, the startup has launched a platform designed to recover whole cloud applications.

Cloud application recovery startup Dreeze announced on Tuesday that it raised $33 million in a seed funding round as it emerged from stealth mode with a platform built to bring back whole cloud applications instead of only the data behind them.
The round was led by Norwest and Bessemer Venture Partners, with Claltech also investing.
Dreeze , whose staff is split between Israel and the United States, said the money will go toward product development, bigger sales and marketing teams, and getting its platform into more enterprises.
The company was formed in 2025 by Avi Raichel and brothers Ziv and Oded Kedem. The three previously worked together at Zerto, which HPE acquired , and Kashya.
Dreeze’s argument is that getting data back after an incident is not the same as getting an application running again. A cyberattack or a mistake by an AI agent can leave an organization with its data intact but without the configurations, secrets, infrastructure and connections the application needs.
Its platform, named Application Revival, scans the customer’s cloud environment on an ongoing basis, works out which resources and dependencies belong to which application, and generates a recovery plan from the live environment. Backups of data and configurations are stored with those recovery plans in an immutable, isolated vault under the customer’s control.
Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.
In a recovery scenario, Application Revival automatically reconstructs the application as a whole. Customers can also run recovery tests in an isolated account, with no impact on production.
“Companies have spent years getting better at backing up data, but getting the data back doesn’t mean the business is back,” said Ziv Kedem, the company’s CEO. “With cyber threats increasing and AI introducing new risks, enterprises need to assume that critical applications will go down.”
“We started Dreeze because recovery needs to go further. Our goal is to make Application Revival the new standard, so companies know they have a proven path to bring their applications back when something goes wrong,” he added.
The AWS version of the platform is generally available. Support for Microsoft Azure is in early access, with general availability expected in early 2027.

Anaergia: C$30 Million Credit Facility Expansion With National Bank Of Canada Increases Financing Capacity By 50%
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 4:47 PM
Anaergia: C$30 Million Credit Facility Expansion With National Bank Of Canada Increases Financing Capacity By 50%
Anaergia, a global technology company specializing in renewable natural gas and organic waste conversion, has expanded its revolving credit facility with National Bank of Canada by 50%, increasing its maximum borrowing capacity from C$20 million to C$30 million. The additional C$10 million in potential financing capacity will support the company’s working capital requirements as it executes its contracted project backlog and converts existing orders into revenue.
The amended agreement builds on the revolving credit facility originally announced on May 6, 2026.
The expansion provides Anaergia with additional financial flexibility to manage the expenditures associated with delivering renewable energy and waste management projects.
The amount available for borrowing at any particular time will remain subject to the facility’s borrowing base and other terms of the credit agreement.
Consequently, the increase in the maximum facility size does not necessarily mean that the entire C$30 million is immediately available for withdrawal.
Amounts borrowed under the facility may be used for general corporate purposes, subject to the agreement’s provisions.
Supporting Project Execution And Working Capital
Anaergia develops and delivers technologies that convert organic waste into valuable products, including renewable natural gas, fertilizer, and water.
Its business encompasses project design, equipment supply, construction, and operational services.
These projects can involve substantial engineering and equipment requirements, creating working capital needs throughout development and implementation.
The expanded credit facility is intended to support these requirements as Anaergia advances its contracted project portfolio.
Working capital is particularly important for businesses delivering large infrastructure and industrial technology projects because expenditures for materials, equipment, labor, and other activities may occur before customers make corresponding payments.
Revolving credit arrangements provide access to financing that can be drawn and repaid as needed, within the limitations of the applicable agreement.
By increasing its maximum borrowing capacity, Anaergia is seeking to improve its ability to manage project-related cash requirements.
Management identified the conversion of its contracted backlog into recognized revenue as a central operating priority.
The additional financing capacity is intended to support that objective while allowing the company to continue its focus on disciplined project execution.
Expanding Renewable Natural Gas And Waste Conversion Infrastructure
Anaergia provides integrated solutions designed to help municipalities, utilities, and industrial organizations manage organic waste more effectively.
Its technologies convert waste streams into renewable energy and other reusable products.
Renewable natural gas is commonly produced by processing biogas generated from the decomposition of organic materials.
After treatment and upgrading, the resulting gas can be used as an energy source in applications that would otherwise rely on conventional natural gas.
Anaergia also develops solutions that recover useful materials from waste processing operations.
These capabilities can help infrastructure operators reduce greenhouse gas emissions while improving the economic value of organic waste and wastewater treatment activities.
The company holds hundreds of patents and has experience delivering complex waste conversion projects internationally.
Its customers include organizations seeking to modernize waste management infrastructure, increase resource recovery, and develop renewable energy production capabilities.
The expanded credit facility provides additional potential financial resources to support Anaergia’s delivery obligations as demand for these solutions develops.
National Bank Of Canada’s Financing Support
National Bank of Canada is one of the country’s six systemically important banks.
As of July 31, 2026, the institution reported approximately C$635 billion in assets.
The bank employs more than 37,000 people and operates businesses spanning personal and commercial banking, wealth management, capital markets, U.S. specialty finance, and international financial services.
Its relationship with Anaergia provides financing infrastructure supporting the company’s project-based operating model.
The increase in maximum revolving credit capacity to C$30 million represents a further expansion of that relationship.
For Anaergia, the amendment strengthens its potential liquidity resources without changing the company’s core focus on renewable natural gas and waste-to-value solutions.
The company intends to use the additional flexibility to manage project delivery, support working capital requirements, and pursue the conversion of its existing contracted backlog into revenue.
KEY QUOTES
“The increase in the maximum principal amount of our revolving credit facility provides Anaergia with additional financial flexibility as we execute our contracted project portfolio. The additional capacity supports the working-capital requirements associated with delivering our projects and reinforces our focus on converting our contracted backlog into revenue through disciplined execution.”
Assaf Onn, CEO Of Anaergia

candidates.snippet: With $23M in funding, Luminal is the latest startup to put Nvidia's CUDA moat in its crosshairs SiliconANGLE
